A card's words describe its own subject, not the session that wrote it
why: A card is read later, cold, by someone who needs to act on its subject. Session facts (who said what, what came before, what stage the conversation was at) are stale on arrival and carry no decision weight.

No planning-process narration in a title, why, or body: no "Eryk said", no "the next thing to prove", no comparison to where the conversation stands.

This includes a card's own edit history. "X is new", "Y used to say/name Z", "that no longer holds/applies" still narrate the session, even when the subject is the card itself. State the current fact plainly. The same holds for where the text came from: "moved here from #x", "split out of #y", "merged from #z". The log records the move; the card states the fact.

A reversal is still fair game to record — a superseded card can say what replaced it and why the earlier reading was wrong — but as a fact about the subject, not a play-by-play of the conversation that produced it. Attribution lives in the "who" field and in the log, not in prose.

A card stays at the level of the decision. It names behaviour and concepts. It does not name a command or a flag: the command form of an operation lives on one card under #werk-cli, and every other card names the operation instead. It does not name source files, functions, classes, constants, line numbers, or internal endpoints. Those change with every refactor, and the card would go stale while its decision still holds. The code points to the card, not the other way round.

The map records decisions that hold for any module, not results for one module. Applying a rule to one module — its behaviour list, its coverage threshold, its test plan — produces an artifact, not a decision. That artifact lives next to the code it describes, in the module's own tests. A card for one module is fair only when that module raises a real design fork the general rule cannot settle.

A card does not list its child cards. The refines edges hold that list, and the map draws it under the card. A copy in the body is a second list that catches up only later: a child that is added, moved, or removed leaves the copy wrong, and no mark shows it. A card states its own higher-level fact. When a sentence states a fact that a child card expands, it names that child in parentheses after the fact. A bullet list or a numbered list in a body is a last resort in general. A list whose items mirror the children is never correct, even when each item is a short fact with the child in parentheses.

A card reads in three layers: the title, the why, and the body
why: The title tells a reader what the card is about. The why gives most of the understanding, so a reader can stop there. The body holds the details for the reader who needs to act.

**Title**

- A plain sentence with a subject and a verb. More words are fine when they make it easier to read.
- One idea. A second clause moves down to the why.
- High level: no mechanism, no tool or subagent names, no "now".
- Name the members of a small set, not a slogan: "Four link types: refines, depends_on, supported_by, alternative_to".

**Why**

- Two or three short sentences. A reader who stops here understands about 80% of the card.
- It gives the reason in plain causal steps, not as an aphorism.
- No card references and no commands. Those go in the body.

**Body**

- Short paragraphs and bullet lists. One item or one option per bullet.
- References to other cards, examples, and ASCII diagrams go here.
- A general overview. It does not repeat the titles of subcards, because the tree shows them.
- Every paragraph helps a reader decide or act. A paragraph that does not is cut.
- A rejected alternative is an option node, not prose.

**Every layer**

- No coined phrases. "Fans out a calm mark" becomes "puts a grey mark on the cards that depend on it".
- When a layer is too long, its content moves down one level: title, then why, then body, then a subcard.

An amend at the end of a review marks the next hop, and its trace says amended
why: A review that changes the card is a change too, so the cards next to it need a mark and a trace. The review sentence is the why that the reader of the trace sees.

A review is the check of one stale card against the change that made it stale (#rederive-reason). It ends in a confirm or an amend. The review records its outcome and one sentence that says why.

A confirm clears the marks on the reviewed card and changes nothing else. An amend clears the marks on the reviewed card that are older than it, and puts a stale mark on its direct dependents and direct children. The trace of each reads: amended, the reviewed card as the cause, and the sentence of the amend (#vi-prop-trace-reason). An amend is a change like any other, so it spreads one hop only (#vi-prop).

Example. Four cards:
- X is "We charge per seat".
- Y is "The invoice shows the seat count". It depends on X.
- Z is "The invoice PDF has a seat column". It depends on Y.
- W is "The invoice has a seat limit line". It is a child of Y.

What happens:
1. X changes to per-usage charging. Y goes stale.
2. The reviewer of Y decides that Y must change. The reviewer ends the review with an amend and writes "The invoice now shows usage units."
3. Y clears. Z and W go stale, and their trace shows that sentence.
4. Nothing else is marked. Each stale card is reviewed in turn.
5. If the reviewer confirms Y instead, Y clears and Z and W stay clear.

```
 Y --depends_on--> X
 Z --depends_on--> Y
 W --refines-----> Y

 X changes                    Y stale.  Z and W clear.
 review of Y: confirm         Y clears. Z and W clear.
 review of Y: amend           Y clears. Z stale. W stale.
   "The invoice now shows usage units."

 trace on Z:   STALE from #Y, amended, <date>
                 The invoice now shows usage units.
                 Z -> Y: <the link reason>
```
